reason: The sources provide over 15 double-verified facts including technical specs, mission timeline, and scientific discoveries.
story: On July 4, 2005, NASA celebrated Independence Day by intentionally smashing an 820-pound copper projectile into Comet Tempel 1 at 23,000 miles per hour. This "Deep Impact" mission used a two-part spacecraft: a Flyby mothership and a smart Impactor. The probe was made of copper to avoid contaminating scientific readings, as copper wasn't expected to be found in a comet. The collision released kinetic energy equivalent to five tons of TNT, creating a massive dust cloud visible to telescopes like Hubble. Initially, scientists struggled with a blurry camera, but they used mathematical "deconvolution" to fix the images. The mission revealed that the comet's interior was much dustier and less icy than predicted, containing organic materials—the building blocks of life. Years later, a second mission confirmed the impact left a crater 150 meters wide. This daring collision provided the first-ever look inside a comet, proving these icy travelers carry the ancient ingredients of our solar system.
angle: NASA celebrated the 4th of July by smashing an 820-pound copper projectile into a comet at 23,000 mph just to see what was hidden inside.

claims.claim: The Deep Impact spacecraft was launched on January 12, 2005.
The Impactor successfully collided with Comet Tempel 1 on July 4, 2005.
The mission utilized a two-part spacecraft consisting of a Flyby section and an Impactor section.
The Impactor section weighed approximately 820 pounds (370-372 kilograms).
The Impactor struck the comet at a relative speed of approximately 23,000 miles per hour.
The projectile was made primarily of copper.
Copper was used for the Impactor to avoid interfering with scientific measurements of the comet's composition.
The kinetic energy of the impact was equivalent to approximately 5 tons of TNT.
The Impactor took its final photo just seconds before it was destroyed by the collision.
The impact created a large dust cloud that initially obscured the view of the resulting crater.
The mission revealed the comet's interior was dustier and less icy than scientists had predicted.
Scientists discovered organic materials, which are considered ingredients for life, inside the comet.
The spacecraft's High Resolution Imager was initially found to be out of focus or blurry.
A mathematical technique called deconvolution was used to fix the blurry images sent from the spacecraft.
NASA's Great Observatories, including Hubble, Spitzer, and Chandra, all observed the impact event.
The European Rosetta spacecraft also monitored the impact from a distance.
The primary goal of the mission was to study the interior composition of a cometary nucleus.
Deep Impact was a part of NASA's low-cost Discovery Program.
In 2011, the Stardust spacecraft visited the site and measured the impact crater at about 150 meters wide.
The comet released millions of kilograms of water and dust as a result of the impact.

disputed: The exact mass of the Impactor is cited as 370 kg in S3 and 372 kg in S1; the script should use 'roughly 370 kilograms'.
The timing of the final image is cited as 3.7 seconds before impact in S1 and 3 seconds in S5; the script should say 'seconds before impact'.
The exact TNT equivalent varies between 4.5-4.8 tons in S1 and 5 tons in S6; the script should use 'approximately five tons'.
The initial crater size was estimated or unknown at first, with S6 predicting stadium-sized; the final 150-meter measurement was only confirmed years later by the Stardust mission.
